content.title: About
content.content: Guava is a tropical fruit native to Central and South America and also cultivated in Southeast Asia. A ripe fruit has a fragrant, mildly sweet flavor with hints of strawberry and citrus, soft yellow‑green flesh, and edible seeds.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Guava is extremely rich in vitamin C: one fruit provides over 200 % of the daily requirement.
The seeds are edible and contain beneficial fatty acids.
In ancient cultures guava was used in traditional medicine to treat colds and digestive issues.
Fruits can be green or yellow depending on the variety and ripeness.
Guava is commonly used in juices, jams, desserts, and sauces.

items.title: High vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps maintain satiety, and assists in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients support vision, skin health, and immune function.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to guava.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet varieties have a high natural sugar level, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic fruit, it is advisable to wash or peel the skin thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Guava can be eaten fresh by cutting it in half and scooping out the flesh with a spoon. It is also suitable for juices, smoothies, salads, desserts, and sauces. The skin can be used in jams after heat treatment.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store guava at room temperature if it is not yet ripe, then move it to the refrigerator. In the fridge, a fresh fruit keeps its quality for up to 5 days. Freezing the pulp allows storage for up to 3 months.
